item.title: Announcing .NET 11
item.description:
Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities.

.NET 11 support

.NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with two years of support under the .NET support policy. STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose.Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13

Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026. The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions.

Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote, or browse the conference session playlist.

What’s new in .NET 11

Some of the changes we’re most excited for you to try:

C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies help you express the possible states of your application and handle them with compiler-checked patterns.A Native AOT CLI host and a warm MSBuild server reduce overhead in everyday developer workflows.ASP.NET Core brings asynchronous validation, OpenAPI 3.2, and new capabilities for Blazor and SignalR applications. Experimental Blazor AI components integrate with the Agent User Interaction Protocol (AG-UI) for advanced agentic web experiences.Build AI-powered, agentic applications with Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) for model access, MCP for tool integration, and Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) for agents and workflows.Put agentic development tools to work with .NET Skills for .NET-specific guidance, .NET MAUI DevFlow for inspecting and testing running apps, and the .NET Upgrade canvas for reviewing modernization progress..NET MAUI adopts CoreCLR as its default runtime and improves XAML iteration and native controls.The libraries add built-in Zstandard compression, simpler process execution, richer JSON support, and new ways to work with in-memory data without copying it first.

The what’s new in .NET 11 overview links to the full details. Here are the changes behind those headlines and how to start using them.

LanguagesC# 15

C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions.

Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found:

ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard"); string message = result switch { Product product => $"Found {product.Name}", ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}", }; Console.WriteLine(message); public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name); public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id); public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound);

The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type.

C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies. A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship.

Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax:

HashSet<string> names = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"]; Console.WriteLine(names.Count);

This prints 2: the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry.

Other additions include extension indexers and labeled break and continue. These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work remains in preview; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements.

F# 11

F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably.

The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders.

PlatformSDK

The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it.

The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication.

File-based apps can grow across source files with #:include, and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. dotnet watch adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects.

For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, dotnet test gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options.

Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies.

See what’s new in the SDK and tooling for command examples and configuration.

Runtime and performance

Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples.

The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional SequenceEqual calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic.

Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for Half operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs.

There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS.

As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose.

Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines.

One especially useful result is a clearer live call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure.

Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting net11.0, add:

<PropertyGroup> <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> </PropertyGroup>

You don’t need to enable EnablePreviewFeatures for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it.

AI libraries and tools

The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template. MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package:

dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer

For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator. These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version.

Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease.

For hands-on examples, start with .NET AI Essentials: The Core Building Blocks Explained and continue with our Microsoft Agent Framework walkthrough.

Libraries

The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers.

The Process API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples.

Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in System.IO.Compression. New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries.

Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a Stream: ReadOnlyMemoryStream, WritableMemoryStream, ReadOnlySequenceStream, and StringStream. For example, a pipeline’s segmented ReadOnlySequence<byte> can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer.

System.Text.Json adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application.

LINQ adds FullJoin, which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side.

The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental.

Entity Framework Core 11

Entity Framework Core 11 improves how your model becomes a query and how that query becomes SQL.

EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves GroupBy translation, and translates the new LINQ FullJoin operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ.

Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities.

For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them.

EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes.

Developer tools

The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates.

.NET Skills gives coding agents task-specific guidance from the .NET team. Our .NET Skills introduction explains how to add these skills to your coding agent.

The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code.

For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution.

WorkloadsWeb: ASP.NET Core and Blazor

Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses System.Text.Json, including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an anyOf schema.

This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries.

Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support.

OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version.

For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change.

Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications.

The new CacheView component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page.

Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive. After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior.

Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. QuickGrid and Virtualize add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection.

Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any IChatClient. For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI.

The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation.

The AG-UI .NET SDK introduction covers the protocol’s client and server APIs. Build Agentic UI with the new Blazor AI components puts them together in a working app.

See what’s new in ASP.NET Core for the Blazor features, configuration examples, and compatibility details.

Client: .NET MAUI

.NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime.

Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model.

The UI development loop gets attention, too:

XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a preview feature in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds.Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file.Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture.New mobile test templates and dotnet test device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow.

These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it.

.NET MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle.

Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF

For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK, which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps.

To add UI tests, see UWP and WinUI 3 apps: UI testing with MSTest.

Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates.

These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign.

WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies.

Get started and plan your upgrade

Install the .NET 11 SDK. Use a compatible, up-to-date Visual Studio 2026 installation, or Visual Studio Code with C# Dev Kit.

To create and run a console app:

dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0 dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11

You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features.

For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments:

Update the SDK selection in global.json if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents.Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions.Review the .NET 11 breaking changes, including the updated minimum CPU requirements. Installing a new SDK alone doesn’t retarget your app.Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts.

Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9

.NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements.

If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build.

Thank you for building .NET with us

.NET 11 is the work of over 7,000 contributors. Thank you to everyone who contributed code, tested previews, reported issues, and helped us make better design decisions throughout the year. Your feedback across the previews and release candidates helped shape what we’re shipping today.

The .NET ecosystem continues to grow, with more than 589,000 unique packages on NuGet and over 1.1 trillion package downloads.

Download .NET 11, try it with an application you know well, and join us at .NET Conf to learn directly from the people building it. Share your results and questions in the .NET GitHub discussions.

.name Grandfathered

10 November 2026

We won!

After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely.

This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person.

item.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
item.description:
Hello you fine Internet folks,

Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.

Hope y’all enjoy!

Overview

From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core.Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2.

At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.

Branch Prediction

Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.

The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5.

Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.

When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.

When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.

The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.

Instruction Fetch

Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.

Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.

Execution Engine

The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.

On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.

AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.

On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.

Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.

The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split

In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.

Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.

The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.

The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.

Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.

L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.

Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.

Load/Store

Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.

A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.

SPEC CPU 2026 Performance

The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.

The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.

The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.

Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.

Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.

Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.

The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.

The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.

Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.

The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

Final Words

The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.

However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.

The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.

AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

item.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
item.description:
Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.

Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.

# Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:

Modern Browser APIs: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).

View an example: the navigation-drawer guide.

item.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
item.description:
Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN subscriber-only content] Welcome to LWN.net

The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN. Thank you for visiting LWN.net!

Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

Synaptics and Displaylink

The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.

The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.

A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.

Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.

Vino

He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome." He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve.

Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.

He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:

The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.

From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.

Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the "intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than "have the situation become more formal later". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK.

Cease and desist

On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not "substantially responded" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with "public statements and further development activities". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work.

Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of "any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent", withdrawing submissions of materials "made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization", and to identify in writing every location "in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.

Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "never lit a panel", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.

On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns."

He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to "reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software".

He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "interact with our respective OIN commitments", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. "I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities".

Lothian did not think he could "reasonably provide the signed undertaking" Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.

Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:

As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate.

The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization.

Bateman sent a follow-up letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking "monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with.

Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "ideally with someone qualified to help me read them". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "DisplayLink is not a member of OIN" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.

OIN to the rescue?

Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.

OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components.

I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.

Status

Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. "Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics."

Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: "You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?'"

For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

item.title: What objective is reasoning solving?
item.description:
There’s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it’ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it’s more likely that we’ll arrive at a correct answer.

But this picture doesn’t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping.1 Sometimes the answer even gets worse, as if it’s overthinking.2 If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn’t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?

This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We’ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.

Reasoning as pathfinding#

Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you’ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let’s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.

Consider the problem: “what’s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$”? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.

We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we’ll call $x$. We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn’t.

So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set

$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$

The figure at the top of this post sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.

Since many paths land in $\Scal_x$, the success probability adds up over all of them. Let $\pi(z \mid x)$ be the probability that the model generates the path $z$ given the prompt $x$, and $y(z)$ for the final answer at the end of $z$. The probability of success is the probability of generating each path, times the probability that path lands in $\Scal_x$, summed over every path:

$$p_x = \prob{\text{a path lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = \sum_{z} \underbrace{\pi(z \mid x)}_{\text{samples path } z}\; \underbrace{\prob{y(z) \in \Scal_x \mid z}}_{\text{path } z \text{ lands in }\Scal_x}.$$

The second factor is just 1 if the path lands in $\Scal_x$ and 0 if it doesn’t, so we sum only the probability of paths that land in $\Scal_x$:

$$p_x = \sum_{z} \pi(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} = \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi(z \mid x).$$

We’ll call $p_x$ the success probability. Maximizing this probability means our model will be more likely to sample a path that lands in $\Scal_x$.

Note that there are two ways of increasing this probability. Either the model can sample multiple paths to the same answer, each with a small probability, or the model can sample a single path to the answer with a very high probability. The success probability doesn’t care which one we get, but in practice we might want to prioritize specific paths or ensure diversity in the samples3.

How do we boost our success probability?#Best-of-$k$ sampling#

The simplest way to pathfind is to have the model $\pi$ keep sampling paths $z$ until one lands in $\Scal_x$.

Since we assumed we had a verifier, we can do best-of-$k$ sampling, which samples $k$ paths and looks for a success. Each path misses with probability $1 - p_x$, so all $k$ miss with probability $(1-p_x)^k$, and the success probability rises from $p_x$ to

$$\prob{\text{at least one of } k \text{ paths lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = 1 - \underbrace{(1-p_x)^k}_{\text{all } k \text{ paths miss}}.$$

This is a guaranteed axis of compute-scaling. As long as $p_x > 0$, the success probability increases monotonically as we sample more paths, so spending more compute on more samples always helps, as seen early on by Brown et al. 2024. However, the scaling here is over the number of samples rather than the length of the paths (thinking longer).

Train the model to generate better samples#

So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?

Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and STaR was an early version of it for reasoning.

RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:

$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$

meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.

Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$

which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$

This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.

In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.

This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.

Amortization and generalization#

During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called amortizing the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question.4 Since we train a single model on many prompts, the model can potentially generalize to new prompts it has never seen.

The figure below shows this for four prompts, each with its own $\Scal_x$, and switches between the model before and after training. During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. As the new prompt gets further from the training distribution, its accuracy drops (try dragging it!).

Revisiting some observations about reasoning#

Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.

Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful#

Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.

If we want meaningful chains of thought, we need to adjust the rewards or the training objective.

Reward hacking comes from both the verifier and the sampler#

We also assumed the verifier is never wrong, that $r(x, y)=1$ if and only if $y$ is actually the correct answer to $x$. But in practice the verifier can be imperfect. Then $\Scal_x$, the set of answers the verifier accepts, isn’t the same as the set of correct answers: it can include wrong answers and leave out correct ones. This misspecification opens up regions of $\Scal_x$ that the model might learn to land in even though it’s not what we intended.

Thus reward-hacking comes from an imperfect verifier, which fails to capture what we truly want, as well as an imperfect sampling procedure which fails to stay away from these shortcut regions.

In the figure below, the dashed circle is the set of correct answers and the red ellipse is $\Scal_x$. The ellipse stretches back toward the prompt, so its wrong answers are the easiest to reach, and after training most paths land there.

This visualization also shows why scaling up RL (generating more samples and longer samples) makes reward hacking more likely. The more extensively we “fuzz” the verifier, the more likely we’ll find a path that lands in the misspecified region of $\Scal_x$. Once the model finds this shortcut, training pushes the model towards similar behavior.

So what objective is reasoning solving?#

Reasoning isn’t actually solving any objective at all. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. It’s only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success.

RL training directly raises the success probability $p_x$, by spending a lot of compute on searching for successful paths and then training the model to reproduce them. Thinking longer helps because training taught the model to use the extra tokens, not because generating more tokens is intrinsically better. The cost of sampling during RL is amortized into the weights. At inference time the model is likely to succeed with a single sample, but any individual sample is not guaranteed to succeed.

Muennighoff et al. 2025 forced a model to keep thinking by appending “Wait” whenever it tried to stop. Accuracy rose at first, and then flattened. ↩︎

A neat example is Gema et al. 2025 which found tasks where longer reasoning resulted in worse accuracy. ↩︎

We might revisit this in a future post. ↩︎

This idea of using expensive search to find a better answer and then training a network to output the answer cheaply, shows up outside language models too. AlphaZero runs a tree search at every move of self-play and trains its policy network to prefer the moves that were found (expert iteration is the same idea). Physicists and weather forecasters do it with simulators: they run an expensive hand-crafted simulation to get an answer, then train a neural network to predict that answer directly. ↩︎

Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America
item.description:
When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back.

Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features.

“Okei,” let’s go.

Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future.

With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses.

The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard.

It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.

The Hybrid Side-By-Side

Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept.

The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle (click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public.

Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car.

In Six Math Essentials, the renowned mathematician and Fields Medalist Terence Tao introduces readers to six central concepts that have guided mathematicians from antiquity to the frontiers of what we know today and now help us make sense of our complex world. This slim, elegant volume explores numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking; algebra as the gateway to abstraction; geometry as a way to calculate beyond what we can see; probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking; analysis as a means to tame the very large or the very small; and dynamics as the mathematics of change.

item.description:
$30M Raised to Redo the CPU

As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing.

Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software.

Tendrils is answering the question: what if we redo the CPU? Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine, which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures.

We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman.
